chapter_title: Input Management and Basic Player Control

screens.title: Input Management & Basic Player Control
screens.subtitle: How Unity reads keys, axes, and mouse movement to drive physics-based characters

narration.text: In this chapter you'll learn how Unity turns physical key presses, mouse motion, and controller sticks into input your game can use. We focus on Unity's built-in Input Manager because it defines the core ideas you will reuse later: named axes for continuous values and named buttons for discrete actions. You will see how polling input every frame and then applying motion in the physics loop creates consistent, responsive movement. As a concrete outcome you'll build a simple PlayerController that reads horizontal and vertical axes, queues a jump with a button press, and uses mouse movement for looking around. I'll point out common pitfalls along the way, such as applying physics from Update or forgetting to normalize diagonal movement, and I will also briefly explain why Unity's newer Input System can be useful for complex projects. By the end of this chapter you'll have both the vocabulary and a practical pattern that makes player control predictable, testable, and ready for extension. Ready to explore real code and examples that you can drop into a scene?

keyIdea.title: Core insight
keyIdea.text: Gather input each frame, then apply forces or movement in the fixed physics loop for stable, responsive control.

screens.title: Input Manager: Axes and Buttons
screens.subtitle: Understand named axes and buttons as the mapping layer

narration.text: The Input Manager is Unity's mapping layer that connects physical controls to named inputs your code can read. An axis is a continuous value, often used for movement or camera control. Think of Horizontal returning a number between minus one and one when you press left or right. A button is a discrete switch that is either on or off; jumping is typically a button. Learning this distinction clarifies which Input methods to call. For example, use the Input GetAxis method to read a smoothed float for player walking and use GetButtonDown to detect the instant the jump is pressed. A concrete example: map Horizontal to A and D and the left stick, then call the Input GetAxis method and use the result to calculate movement. A common misconception is treating an axis like a button. That mistake leads to logic that expects true or false when the axis actually returns a range, and it complicates actions like single-press jumps. Key takeaway: name your axes and buttons clearly and pick the input method that matches continuous or discrete behavior. How will you name a new sprint control so it can map to both a key and a controller button?

keyIdea.title: Definition
keyIdea.text: Axis = continuous float between -1 and 1. Button = discrete true or false for single actions.

content.html:
Module 3 › Chapter 2.5 › Axes and Buttons
What is an Axis?
An axis returns a float value often from minus one to one. Use it for continuous motion and analog input like joystick sticks or mouse delta.
What is a Button?
A button yields a boolean. It's ideal for single events such as jumping, firing, or opening a menu.
Example
Map Horizontal to keys and sticks. Use the Input GetAxis method and multiply the value by speed to move the player smoothly.
Misconception
Treating an axis like a button causes logic errors. Don't compare an axis to true; compare its numeric value instead.
Visual
Axis: Horizontal
Value range: -1 .. 0 .. 1
Button: Jump
State: pressed or not pressed
Key Takeaway

Pick axis methods for analog values and button methods for single events to match gameplay intent.

screens.title: GetAxis vs GetAxisRaw
screens.subtitle: Smoothing versus immediate input and when to choose each

narration.text: Unity provides two similar methods for reading named axes: the Input GetAxis method and Input GetAxisRaw. The GetAxis method smooths values over time, which creates a gentler acceleration and deceleration. This smoothing can help movement feel more natural for third person or platforming games where abrupt changes look jarring. By contrast, GetAxisRaw returns only minus one, zero, or one without smoothing, giving you immediate, non interpolated values. Use the raw variant when you need crisp, snappy control such as in precise platformers or input that drives instant rotation. A concrete example: if the player is moving and you rely on GetAxis smoothing, stopping input may produce a small glide as the axis interpolates back to zero. If you want instant stop, switch to GetAxisRaw or handle smoothing manually. A common pitfall is assuming smoothing fixes physics problems; it only affects the input value. Always pair your input decision with the correct physics handling and normalization to avoid conflicting forces. Consider which feel you want before picking one, then test in Play Mode. GetAxis vs GetAxisRaw means getaxis smooths values for gentle movement; getaxisraw gives immediate, unsmoothed control for sharper responses.. In practical terms, smoothing versus immediate input and when to choose each. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

keyIdea.title: Choice
keyIdea.text: GetAxis smooths values for gentle movement; GetAxisRaw gives immediate, unsmoothed control for sharper responses.

content.html:

GetAxis (smoothed)
Provides interpolated floats useful for natural transitions and eased movement.
Example
Use it for camera orbit or smooth character acceleration where instant stops feel abrupt.
Pro tip: smoothing is cosmetic for input; physics must still be handled in FixedUpdate.
GetAxisRaw (immediate)
Returns -1, 0, or 1 for exact controller or key states, without interpolation.
Example
Choose raw input for precise movement or grid based controls where latency matters.
Check
If movement feels slippery, try the raw axis or normalize and control acceleration explicitly.
Key Takeaway
Pick smoothing based on game feel. GetAxis for eased motion; GetAxisRaw for immediate response.

screens.title: Button and Key Methods
screens.subtitle: When to use GetButton, GetButtonDown, GetKey and GetKeyDown

narration.text: Unity exposes a set of methods for discrete input events. Use the GetButton method to check if a configured virtual button is held; this is helpful for continuous actions tied to a named mapping. Use GetButtonDown when you want the action to fire only on the frame the button is pressed. That makes it ideal for jump triggers and single shots. Similarly, GetKey returns true every frame a specific physical keyboard key is held, while GetKeyDown returns true only in the initial press frame. A concrete scenario: implement a jump that should only happen once per press by using GetButtonDown for the mapped Jump virtual button or GetKeyDown for the spacebar key code. A common misunderstanding is using GetButton for jump logic, which will trigger repeatedly if you do not guard it with grounded checks; this leads to infinite jumping. The correct pattern is to detect the press in Update, set a request flag, and then process that request in FixedUpdate where the physics are safe. This prevents repeated triggers and keeps input detection responsive. Button and Key Methods means getbutton and getkey check continuous hold. use down variants for single-frame triggers like jump.. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

Module 3 › Chapter 2.5 › Button and Key Methods
Continuous checks
Use GetButton or GetKey to know if an input remains held. Good for sprinting while a key is pressed.
Single-press checks
Use the Down variants to trigger an action only once at the initial press moment.
Concrete example
To implement a sprint toggle, use GetKey for Left Shift so the player runs while the key is held. For a jump, use GetButtonDown or GetKeyDown to ensure one jump per press.
Common mistake
Checking GetButton every frame without a grounded guard can allow repeated jumps. Use a flag and process the jump in FixedUpdate.
Key Takeaway

Choose hold checks for continuous input and Down checks for single, immediate triggers.

screens.title: Update vs FixedUpdate Pattern
screens.subtitle: Gather inputs each frame, apply physics on fixed ticks

narration.text: A reliable pattern for physics based control separates input gathering from physics application. Unity's Update runs every frame and is the correct place to poll input because it aligns with the display and captures every press. FixedUpdate runs on a fixed time step and is where you should apply forces or move the Rigidbody to keep physics deterministic. The pattern is simple: read axis values and discrete presses in Update, store those results in private fields, and then in FixedUpdate use those stored values to call MovePosition or AddForce. For example, read the horizontal and vertical axis into a move direction vector in Update and set a jumpRequested flag on GetButtonDown. In FixedUpdate compute the target position using the stored vector and use the Rigidbody MovePosition method, and if jumpRequested is true, apply an impulse and clear the flag. A common error is calling physics methods directly inside Update; this causes non uniform physics behavior across different frame rates. The practical benefit is stable movement and consistent collision responses. Try asking: if movement still feels jittery, which part of the pattern should you inspect first?

keyIdea.title: Pattern
keyIdea.text: Read input in Update and apply movement in FixedUpdate to keep physics consistent across frame rates.

content.html:
Module 3 › Chapter 2.5 › Update vs FixedUpdate
Step 1 — Gather Input
In Update read axes and button presses. Store results in private variables for later use.
Step 2 — Apply Physics
In FixedUpdate use stored input values to call MovePosition or AddForce on the Rigidbody.
Analogy: Update is the sensor, FixedUpdate is the actuator that runs on a steady beat.
Example flow
  1. Read Horizontal and Vertical into a move vector in Update.
  2. If Jump is pressed set jumpRequested true in Update.
  3. In FixedUpdate MovePosition using the stored vector.
  4. If jumpRequested then AddForce up and clear the flag.
Common mistake
Applying physics in Update causes frame-rate dependent movement and inconsistent collisions.

screens.title: PlayerController: Movement and Jump Pattern
screens.subtitle: A practical script that separates input and physics

narration.text: Let's walk through the typical PlayerController that uses the Input Manager and Rigidbody movement. The essential idea is to read axis values and button presses in Update, store them, and then in FixedUpdate call Rigidbody MovePosition and AddForce for jumping. In practice you read Horizontal and Vertical with the Input GetAxis method, compute a move direction relative to the player's transform, normalize to avoid faster diagonal movement, and store that vector in a private field. When the virtual Jump button is pressed and the player is grounded, set a jumpRequested flag. In FixedUpdate compute the target position by adding the move vector multiplied by speed and fixed delta time to the current position, then call MovePosition. If jumpRequested is set, apply an upward impulse and clear the flag. The script also checks that the Rigidbody component exists during Awake and logs an error if not. A common misconception is normalizing after multiplying by speed; normalization should occur before scaling so diagonal speed matches cardinal speed. Test this in a scene with a plane tagged Ground and a capsule with a Rigidbody to validate behavior.

keyIdea.title: Pattern code
keyIdea.text: Read input in Update, normalize move direction, then MovePosition and AddForce in FixedUpdate while using a jump request flag.

content.html:

// Update: read Input GetAxis for Horizontal and Vertical
// Store move vector and set jumpRequested on GetButtonDown("Jump")
// FixedUpdate: compute targetPosition = rb.position + moveDirection * moveSpeed * Time.fixedDeltaTime
// rb.MovePosition(targetPosition)
// if jumpRequested then rb.AddForce(up * jumpForce, impulse) and clear flag
This pseudocode follows the recommended pattern. Keep input collection in Update for responsiveness and call physics on FixedUpdate for determinism.
Concrete example
In a scene with a capsule tagged Player and a plane tagged Ground, attach this script and test walking and single press jumping.
Pitfall
If you forget to normalize the move vector diagonal speed becomes larger than cardinal speed.
Key Takeaway
Keep the input to physics separation and normalize direction before applying speed.

screens.title: Ground Check and Collision Handling
screens.subtitle: Ensuring a single jump and reliable grounded state

narration.text: Ground checking is the mechanism that prevents multiple jumps and confirms when the player can apply grounded logic. A common simple approach checks collisions: when a collision occurs with an object tagged Ground set isGrounded true, and when exiting that collision set it false. This method assumes your ground objects use the Ground tag and that colliders and rigidbodies are configured to detect collisions. A more robust pattern uses a short raycast downward or a small sphere overlap to check for ground contact beneath the character; that avoids missing a ground contact when colliders are small or the player moves quickly. A concrete example from the PlayerController script uses OnCollisionEnter and OnCollisionExit with a tag check to set the grounded flag. A common misconception is to rely on collision normal alone; while helpful, normals can vary on slopes so combine tag checks with positional checks if needed. Key takeaway: choose a ground detection approach that matches your level geometry and test on slopes and steps. What test will reveal whether your ground detection works on uneven terrain? Ground Check and Collision Handling means use collision tag checks, raycasts, or sphere overlaps to maintain a reliable grounded state and prevent multiple jumps.. In practical terms, ensuring a single jump and reliable grounded state. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

keyIdea.title: Grounding
keyIdea.text: Use collision tag checks, raycasts, or sphere overlaps to maintain a reliable grounded state and prevent multiple jumps.

content.html:
Module 3 › Chapter 2.5 › Ground Check & Collisions
Collision based ground check
Use OnCollisionEnter to set isGrounded when colliding with objects tagged Ground and OnCollisionExit to clear it.
Raycast or sphere check
Cast a short downward ray or sphere to detect ground contact under the player; this is often more reliable on slopes or thin colliders.
Tip: Tune ray length or sphere radius to the player's collider size to avoid false negatives.
Concrete scenario
In a level with steps, collision events may flicker. A short sphere check under the character center gives a stable grounded result.
Misconception
Assuming collision normals always indicate ground will fail on thin geometry or edge cases. Combine checks for robustness.
Key Takeaway
Choose the ground detection that fits your level geometry and test on slopes and jumps to validate behavior.

screens.title: Mouse Look: Horizontal Player Rotation and Camera Pitch
screens.subtitle: Capture mouse axes and clamp camera rotation for comfortable control

narration.text: Mouse look adds rotation input to your player and camera using the same Input Manager axes. Read the Mouse X and Mouse Y axes in Update multiplied by a mouse sensitivity variable and by time scaled appropriately. For horizontal rotation rotate the player transform around the Y axis using the mouse X value so movement direction and view remain aligned. For vertical rotation, adjust a camera local rotation variable and clamp it between sensible values such as minus ninety and ninety degrees to avoid flipping the camera. A concrete implementation uses a stored xRotation float that subtracts the mouse Y input, clamps it, and applies it to the camera local rotation while applying mouse X directly to the player's Y rotation. Remember to lock and hide the cursor using the Cursor lock state for an immersive experience during Play Mode. A common error is applying camera pitch to the player transform instead of the camera, which causes awkward roll and misaligned aiming. Test the sensitivity and clamps to find a comfortable feel for your game. Mouse Look: Horizontal Player Rotation and Camera Pitch means use mouse x to rotate the player and mouse y to pitch the camera, clamping pitch to avoid flipping.. In practical terms, capture mouse axes and clamp camera rotation for comfortable control. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

keyIdea.title: Mouse look
keyIdea.text: Use Mouse X to rotate the player and Mouse Y to pitch the camera, clamping pitch to avoid flipping.

content.html:
Module 3 › Chapter 2.5 › Mouse Look
Pattern
Read Mouse X and Mouse Y in Update, multiply by sensitivity and Time delta, rotate player around Y for horizontal look, update camera local X rotation for pitch and clamp it to prevent inversion.
// Read mouse inputs in Update and scale by sensitivity
// Apply horizontal rotation to the player transform using mouse X
// Update a stored xRotation by subtracting mouse Y, clamp it, and set camera local rotation
// Lock the cursor to center while testing
Concrete steps
  1. Expose mouseSensitivity and a camera Transform in the script.
  2. Multiply Mouse X and Mouse Y by sensitivity and Time delta in Update.
  3. Use transform Rotate for horizontal and camera localRotation for vertical pitch.
  4. Clamp pitch between -90 and 90 degrees for comfort.
Misconception
Applying vertical rotation to the player object instead of the camera causes the whole body to tilt and breaks movement alignment.

screens.title: Hands-on Activity: Enhancing Player Movement with Mouse Look
screens.subtitle: Step-by-step lab you can run in Play Mode

narration.text: This activity walks through a practical enhancement: add mouse look to the PlayerController and test movement. Start with a scene containing a Plane tagged Ground and a Capsule named Player with a Rigidbody. Make the Main Camera a child of the Player so it follows rotation. screens.title: Common Mistakes and Best Practices
screens.subtitle: Avoiding jitter, infinite jumps, and inconsistent physics

narration.text: When implementing input based control there are several recurring mistakes to watch for. First, applying physics in Update rather than FixedUpdate produces inconsistent forces and jitter across machines with different frame rates. Second, not normalizing the movement vector before scaling by speed makes diagonal movement faster than straight movement. Third, checking for jump with hold checks instead of single-press checks can produce infinite jumping if grounded logic is missing. Fourth, using the wrong axis smoothing can change game feel unexpectedly; choose GetAxisRaw when immediate response matters. Best practices that address these pitfalls include: read inputs in Update and stash them, normalize direction vectors before applying speed, process jump requests in FixedUpdate with a grounded guard, and test on slopes and at variable frame rates. For networked games validate input on the server to avoid cheating. The practical test is to run Play Mode at different frame rates and on slopes to see if movement remains consistent. Which of these mistakes have you run into before and how did you fix it? This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

Mistake: Using hold checks for single actions

Practical fixes

  • Normalize direction vectors before scaling by speed to keep consistent velocity.
  • Use Down checks for single events and verify grounded status before jumping.

screens.title: The New Input System — A Brief Note
screens.subtitle: Why you might choose the modern package for complex projects

narration.text: Unity's newer Input System is an alternate package that offers action maps, control schemes, and event driven input. It excels when you need remapping, multiple device profiles, or a declarative workflow that separates input devices from in game actions. The legacy Input Manager remains simpler and widely used; understanding it forms a solid foundation and is often sufficient for many projects and exam scenarios. A concrete reason to prefer the new system is when supporting many different controllers and custom remapping without writing extensive device handling code. A common misunderstanding is that the new system always replaces the legacy one; in fact projects can use either depending on their needs. For this chapter you should be comfortable with the built in Input Manager because it exposes the core ideas of axes and buttons. When starting a new large scale project, evaluate the new Input System for its flexibility, but keep the legacy patterns in your toolkit for compatibility and quick iteration. The New Input System — A Brief Note means the new input system offers action maps and better device support; the legacy input manager remains useful and exam relevant.. In practical terms, why you might choose the modern package for complex projects. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

keyIdea.text: The new Input System offers action maps and better device support; the legacy Input Manager remains useful and exam relevant.

Choose it for projects requiring many device types, runtime remapping, or complex input flows across platforms.
Concrete comparison
Legacy Input Manager is quick and well suited to simple setups. The new system is more flexible but requires setup through the Package Manager and action maps.
Key Takeaway
Know both systems: legacy for quick work and exam relevance, new system for advanced device support and remapping.

screens.title: Key Concepts
screens.subtitle: What to remember from this chapter

narration.text: To wrap up, keep three compact concepts in mind. First, the Input Manager maps physical controls to named axes and buttons; axes are for continuous float values and buttons are for discrete actions. Second, adopt the Update then FixedUpdate pattern: gather input each frame and apply movement or forces on fixed physics ticks to ensure consistent behavior. Third, choose the proper input method for your use case: smoothing with GetAxis, immediate response with GetAxisRaw, and single press with GetButtonDown or GetKeyDown. These practices prevent common problems like inconsistent physics, faster diagonal movement, and infinite jumps. Also be aware that Unity provides a new Input System for more advanced needs, but the legacy system taught here remains important for many projects and for exam scenarios. Use these key concepts as a checklist the next time you implement player control.

narration.text: Keep this quick reference handy while you code. Axis means a floating value typically between minus one and one used for movement and camera input. Button refers to a boolean state useful for actions like jumping or firing. The GetAxisRaw method returns immediate -1, 0, or 1 values while GetAxis returns smoothed floats. Use GetButtonDown or GetKeyDown for single press detection and GetButton or GetKey for continuous checks. Finally, always read input in Update and apply forces or MovePosition in FixedUpdate to keep physics behavior consistent. A simple real-world example is helpful here, because students learn best when they can connect the idea to a familiar situation. This matters because it gives the learner a clear mental model and helps them connect the concept to later examples and problems. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

keyIdea.title: Cheat sheet
keyIdea.text: Axis = float; Button = bool; GetAxisRaw = immediate; GetButtonDown = one time press; Update then FixedUpdate.

Module 3 › Chapter 2.5 › Quick Reference
Axis
Continuous float, use for motion or camera delta.
Button
Discrete action state, use for jump and fire.
Timing
Read in Update, apply movement in FixedUpdate for reliable physics.
Final Tip
Test input behavior on slopes and across different frame rates to validate your control feel.
